title: Quantifying Qual Without Losing the Story
intro: Counting how many people mentioned something rewards noisy, low-impact issues and buries rare, severe ones.

topics.title: Quantifying Qual Without Losing the Story

learn.title: Five steps from transcript to evidence
learn.text:
**1. Slice** — one testable claim per evidence unit
**2. Code** — against a codebook tied to decisions: in, out, which decision
**3. Agree** — check two researchers code alike (kappa or alpha), after calibration
**4. Weight** — by severity, segment and evidence quality
**5. Show a range** — not one number, and say what could change it

Overkill for every study. Right when the decision drives a major investment or a critical journey.

try.q: What is the problem with simply counting mentions?
options: Noisy minor issues outrank rare severe ones
Counts are hard to calculate reliably

learn.title: Slicing rules
learn.text:
Rules you can teach in ten minutes:

• **Split on conjunctions that introduce a new claim.** “I search first, and then I browse categories” is two units.
• **Keep cause and effect together.** “The label is vague, so I hesitate” is one unit.
• **Separate speculation from observation and flag it.** “Maybe other teams would like this.”

try.q: “I search first, and then I browse categories.” How many evidence units?
try.explain: The conjunction introduces a second claim.

left.label: One unit
items: “The label is vague, so I hesitate”

right.label: Two units
items: “I search first, and then I browse”

learn.title: Agreement and weighting
learn.text:
Before synthesis, two researchers code the same subset and compare — **after calibration**, not before. Kappa or Krippendorff's alpha gives a number for how much the coding is reproducible.

Then weight by **severity**, **segment** (does it affect the users who matter for this decision?) and **evidence quality**.

Finally show a range and name what could move it, rather than a single confident figure.

try.q: What does rater agreement tell you?
options: Whether the sample was large enough
try.explain: It measures consistency between coders, not correctness.

test.q: When is this level of rigour appropriate?
options: When the decision drives a major investment
When the sample exceeds twenty people
test.explain: Calabro calls it overkill for everyday work.

test.q: What should the codebook be tied to?
test.explain: In, out, and which decision each code serves.

test.q: What should be flagged separately from observation?
test.explain: “Maybe other teams would like this” is not evidence of what happens.

test.q: Which three factors drive the weighting?
test.explain: Weighting is what stops counting from misleading.

test.q: What should the final output show?
options: A range, and what could change it
The number of mentions per theme
